definition: To publicly say that you approve of or support a person, plan, product, or idea.
example: The school nurse endorsed the proposal to start morning classes an hour later.
nuance: Unlike approve, which can be private, endorse usually means declaring support openly so that others may be influenced.
prompt: A respected scientist reviews a new science textbook shortly before it is published.
options: The scientist agreed to endorse the textbook in a short note printed on its back cover.
The scientist chose to endorse the textbook by listing its many errors in a harsh review.
The scientist had to endorse three long hours of a dull meeting about the textbook.
The scientist decided to endorse the textbook by never mentioning it to anyone.
reasons: A public statement of praise that readers will see is exactly this kind of open support.
A harsh review attacks the book, which is the reverse of backing it.
Sitting through something unpleasant is enduring it; this confuses two similar-sounding verbs.
Silence offers no support at all; the word requires an active, visible expression of approval.

practice.prompt: A baker is asked what she thinks of a new flour supplier at a meeting of local shop owners.
options: At the meeting, the baker stood up to endorse the supplier and urged others to try its flour.
The baker wanted to endorse the supplier, so she warned every shop owner to stay away from it.
The baker hopes to endorse the supplier with a large gift of money for a new warehouse.
The baker hired a guard to endorse the market's rule against bringing dogs inside.
reasons: Speaking up in front of peers and recommending the supplier is open, public backing.
Warning people away is criticism, the opposite of lending your support.
Donating funds to an organization is endowing it, a different verb that only looks similar.
Making people obey a rule is enforcing it; the look-alike word does not mean this.
